clinicalPearls: Caused by pathogenic variants in MEFV encoding pyrin, classically autosomal recessive with founder populations across the eastern Mediterranean (Sephardic and Mizrahi Jews, Armenians, Turks, Arabs); M694V homozygosity carries the most severe phenotype and highest amyloidosis risk.
Attacks are short-lived, usually resolving within a few days, and feature fever with self-limiting serositis: sterile peritonitis mimicking an acute abdomen, pleuritis, and less often pericarditis.
Acute monoarthritis of a large lower-limb joint and an erysipelas-like erythema over the ankle, foot or shin are characteristic mucocutaneous and articular manifestations.

Colchicine taken continuously is the cornerstone of therapy, preventing attacks in most patients and, crucially, preventing systemic AA amyloidosis; adherence rather than dose escalation usually explains apparent failure.
Interleukin-1 blockade is reserved for genuinely colchicine-resistant or colchicine-intolerant disease and for established amyloidosis.
Subclinical inflammation with persistently raised serum amyloid A can occur between clinically silent intervals and drives amyloid deposition even when attacks seem controlled.
Protracted febrile myalgia and exercise-induced lower-limb myalgia are recognised variants that can be mistaken for vasculitis or myositis.
A trial of colchicine with a clear symptomatic and biochemical response supports the diagnosis when genetic testing is equivocal.
reference.pathophysiology: Pyrin, the product of the MEFV gene expressed predominantly in innate immune cells, normally acts as a sensor that becomes activated when RhoA-mediated pyrin phosphorylation is lost, as occurs with certain bacterial toxins. Gain-of-function variants lower the threshold for assembly of the pyrin inflammasome, leading to caspase-1 activation, unregulated maturation and release of interleukin-1 beta and interleukin-18, and neutrophil-rich serosal inflammation. The episodic nature reflects intermittent triggering superimposed on a lowered inflammatory set point, while chronic overproduction of serum amyloid A during and between attacks underlies reactive AA amyloidosis, the principal determinant of long-term morbidity.
additionalDifferentials: PFAPA (periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, adenitis) syndrome
Acute surgical abdomen such as appendicitis or perforated viscus
Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and adult-onset Still's disease
additionalInvestigations: Targeted MEFV gene sequencing for pathogenic variants
Acute-phase reactants (C-reactive protein, serum amyloid A, fibrinogen) measured during and between attacks
Serial urinalysis for proteinuria as amyloidosis surveillance
Renal biopsy with Congo red staining when nephrotic-range proteinuria develops
SAA1 genotype where available to refine amyloidosis risk stratification
Cross-sectional imaging during an attack to document serositis and exclude a surgical cause
redFlags: New or increasing proteinuria signalling incipient renal AA amyloidosis
An attack that fails to remit within the usual short window, raising concern for true surgical peritonitis or protracted febrile myalgia
Breathlessness or haemodynamic compromise suggesting pericardial involvement
Persistently elevated inflammatory markers between attacks despite apparent clinical control
reference.prognosis: With adherent colchicine prophylaxis most patients achieve good control of attacks and normal life expectancy, and the risk of amyloidosis falls substantially. Untreated or poorly controlled disease, particularly with high-risk MEFV and SAA1 genotypes, progresses to renal failure from AA amyloidosis.
pitfalls: Recurrent sterile peritonitis leading to unnecessary appendicectomy or laparotomy before the diagnosis is considered
Assuming a negative or heterozygous MEFV result excludes the disease, as phenotype does not always follow a simple recessive pattern and not all pathogenic variants are covered by every panel
Attributing apparent colchicine failure to true resistance rather than to non-adherence or gastrointestinal intolerance
Overlooking silent amyloidosis because attacks are clinically well controlled
references: Firestein & Kelley's Textbook of Rheumatology (current edition)
EULAR recommendations for the management of familial Mediterranean fever
management: Give lifelong continuous colchicine as the cornerstone to prevent attacks and, crucially, to prevent AA amyloidosis, emphasising adherence rather than dose escalation
Reserve interleukin-1 blockade (anakinra or canakinumab) for genuinely colchicine-resistant or colchicine-intolerant disease and for established amyloidosis
Relieve acute serosal attacks with anti-inflammatory analgesia while avoiding unnecessary laparotomy for sterile peritonitis
Surveil for AA amyloidosis with serial urinalysis for proteinuria and monitoring of serum amyloid A and C-reactive protein, even between attacks
Manage nephrotic-range proteinuria and renal amyloidosis with nephrology input, progressing to renal replacement or transplantation if kidney failure develops
Offer genetic counselling with MEFV testing and SAA1 genotype for amyloidosis risk stratification where available
